title: New styles from one block: panels, sleeves and collars

say: New styles from one block: panels, sleeves and collars.
This is the video for module three of Advanced Tailoring and Pattern Making.
Flat-pattern manipulation means changing a tested block on paper to make a new style. Because the block already fits, every new style keeps that fit at the neck, shoulder, bust and waist.

say: With slash and spread, you cut lines on a copy and open them to add width. For a flared skirt, slash from the dart point to the hem and close the dart. The dart becomes flare at the hem.

panel.heading: Slash and spread, or pivot
left: Open the cuts to add width

say: With pivot, you hold the paper down with an awl on the bust point and rotate the block to close a dart. Both give the same result.

panel.heading: Slash and spread, or pivot
left: Open the cuts to add width

say: A princess seam is a full seam over the bust, so each panel can be shaped on its own. For example, Efe in Benin City makes a lace mermaid gown. At the toile fitting the waist is 6 cm too big all round.

panel.heading: Share the change across panels
items: Waist 6 cm too big, bust and hip fine
6 seams, so 12 edges
6 cm ÷ 12 = 0.5 cm per edge
Blend back about 10 cm above and below
Re-true seams; change lining too

say: The gown has front and back princess seams plus two side seams. That is six seams, and twelve edges.

say: The sleeve cap must match the armhole, plus a small planned extra called cap ease. For example, Adaeze in Owerri measures a front armhole of 22 cm and a back of 23.5 cm. Total, 45.5 cm.

panel.heading: Draft the sleeve from the armhole
items: Armhole: 22 + 23.5 = 45.5 cm
Add about 3 cm cap ease: about 48.5 cm
Bicep too narrow? Lower the cap 1 cm
Cap curve 49.5 cm? Flatten near crown
Final cap: 48.6 cm, then test

say: For crepe she wants about 3 cm of cap ease, so the cap curve should be about 48.5 cm.

say: Her first draft gave a bicep of 31 cm, less than the client's 32 cm arm. A lower cap makes a wider sleeve, so she lowers it by 1 cm. The bicep becomes about 34 cm.

say: Every collar starts from the neckline length measured on the pattern. For a mandarin stand, draw a rectangle half the neckline long. Raise the front end of the lower edge by 1 to 1.5 cm, so it hugs the neck.

cards.d: Rectangle, half neckline long. Raise the front end 1 to 1.5 cm so it hugs the neck.
Overlap shoulders 1 to 2 cm at the armhole end. This gives a slight roll that hides the seam.
Stand curves upward; collar curves downward at front. Collar 1 to 1.5 cm deeper at back.

say: For a Peter Pan collar, overlap the shoulders by 1 to 2 cm at the armhole end. That gives a slight roll that hides the seam.

say: For a shirt collar, the stand curves upward but the collar curves downward at the front, and the collar is 1 to 1.5 cm deeper at the back.
Staystitch the neckline right after cutting, so it does not stretch.

say: To remember. Work on a copy of your block. A closed dart can become a yoke, gathers or flare. Share fit changes across all seams.
Draft sleeves from the armhole, and collars from the measured neckline.
